identity.title: Constant epigastric pain radiating to the back (with alcohol/gallstone history)

technique.how: Ask about location (epigastric/upper abdominal), character (constant, severe, boring), onset over minutes to an hour, radiation straight through to the back, relief on sitting forward, associated vomiting, and risk factors: alcohol quantity, known gallstones, recent ERCP, hypertriglyceridaemia, new drugs.

interpretation.positive_finding: Constant severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with alcohol or gallstone history is the classic presentation of acute pancreatitis and fulfils the clinical criterion of the diagnosis when lipase/amylase >3x ULN.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of back radiation does not exclude pancreatitis; many patients have epigastric pain without radiation, and pain may be atypical in the elderly.
interpretation.pitfalls: Same pattern occurs with penetrating posterior peptic ulcer, ruptured/expanding AAA, aortic dissection and inferior MI; tearing pain with pulse deficit or hypotension should trigger aortic imaging first. Grey Turner/Cullen ecchymoses occur in only ~3% of pancreatitis.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: order lipase and consider pancreatitis; if pain is abrupt, tearing, or with hypotension/pulsatile mass, image the aorta before accepting pancreatitis.

sources.citation: Tenner S, Baillie J, DeWitt J, Vege SS. American College of Gastroenterology guideline: management of acute pancreatitis. Am J Gastroenterol. 2013;108(9):1400-1415.
Dickson AP, Imrie CW. The incidence and prognosis of body wall ecchymosis in acute pancreatitis. Surg Gynecol Obstet. 1984;159(4):343-347.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a 'pancreatitis-type' history to defer aortic imaging in a patient with hypotension, pulse deficit, syncope, or a pulsatile mass.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Epigastric-to-back pain with shock, tearing onset, or a pulsatile abdominal mass: treat as AAA/dissection until excluded.

extraction_notes: No diagnostic-accuracy data (sens/spec/LR) for the pain pattern itself were found; PubMed search 'acute pancreatitis pain radiating back sensitivity specificity' returned unrelated or case-report items (e.g. PMID 12094856, 25473197 - not used). The ACG 2013 guideline defines pancreatitis by 2 of 3 criteria including characteristic abdominal pain, cited as guideline source. Dickson & Imrie 1984 (abstract): 'The over-all incidence of 3 per cent is greater than generally appreciated' (Abstract) - frequency of body-wall ecchymosis in 770 pancreatitis patients; a prognostic/frequency figure, not a diagnostic estimate of pain radiation, so no estimate entered.
